string.equality.ref: JavaScript strings are values: two equal strings are never different references. Compare strings with == or string.Equals.
boxing.equality: Values are not boxed in JavaScript: two boxed equal numbers compare equal by reference too. Compare unboxed values instead of relying on reference identity.
float.precision: `float` is a JavaScript number, so it keeps double precision instead of rounding to single. Use `double`, or a Float32Array from WebSharper.JavaScript when single-precision storage matters.
array.outofrange: Array accesses are not bounds-checked: reading past the end gives undefined instead of throwing IndexOutOfRangeException. Check Length before indexing.
exception.null.deref: Dereferencing null throws a JavaScript TypeError, not a NullReferenceException. Check for null (or use ?.) instead of catching NullReferenceException.
dict.insertion.order: After a Remove, .NET reuses the freed slot for the next Add; that order is unspecified in .NET, and JavaScript keeps insertion order. Sort the keys, or use SortedDictionary, when order matters.
generic.default: Generics are erased: default(T) inside generic code is null for value types too. Pass the default value in, or constrain T to a class.
enum.getvalues: Enums are erased to numbers: a boxed or generic enum value formats as its number. Call ToString on the statically typed enum value.
list.capacity.tostring: No runtime type names: Object.ToString on a type that does not override it does not give the .NET type name. Override ToString, or use nameof.
object.tostring.default: No runtime type names: Object.ToString on a type that does not override it does not give the .NET type name. Override ToString, or use nameof.
gettype.name: No reflection: GetType() is not available in JavaScript. Use nameof for names, pattern matching (`is`) for type tests, or WebSharper.JavaScript.Object.GetPrototypeOf for the JavaScript prototype.
span.sum: Span<T> and stackalloc are not supported. Use arrays, or JavaScript typed arrays from WebSharper.JavaScript.
